answer.evidence: The brazier is a flame (decor, rows 0-8) over a bowl band that is 12 px wide for rows 8-11. The width profile does not widen and narrow again, so there is no ellipse. The only top evidence is a 2-row dark-purple glow strip at rows 9-10, which sits just above a dark front-edge line at row 11. That is a rim-level strip, not a visible bowl opening with contents. Below it the pedestal shaft (width 8, rows 12-22) and the flared base (rows 23-26) are drawn as a purely vertical front face of about 15 rows, with no top surface.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a small grey stone pedestal with a purple flame bowl. It has only 9 distinct colours, against 14 for the thin references (bench, lamp) and 38-40 for the well and stall. The stone body shows about 3 tones (light face, mid, dark side) with little per-stone shading or grain. The flame has roughly 3 tones. Beodeul references use 5-6 steps per material and carry texture dots, such as the well's stones shaded one by one. The outline is tinted: 0% of dark edge pixels are neutral, so it reads as a dark bluish-purple material tone and not a black sticker line. There are no large flat fills, since the piece is small and no 5x5 block is flat. The tile-level facts are 0 because the piece is smaller than one tile, so density is judged by eye. By eye the pedestal is simpler and flatter than the well or lamp, with shallow shading and little texture. A careful artist would likely see it as thinner than the references, so it fails.

The whole piece has only 9 distinct colours, against 11-40 for the references; even the thin lamp-crook has 14.
